entries.title: Horrific discovery at South Chicago Chapel raises questions about Illinois funeral home oversight
entries.summary: <p>A macabre discovery in a Far South Side funeral home is once again revealing gaps in government oversight of facilities like the one in South Deering where authorities found dozens of decomposing bodies <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" target="_blank" ><u>last week</u></a>, according to lawmakers who called for state-level reform on Monday.</p><p>But before Springfield takes another swing at the issue, officials were still trying to pin down who could have prevented the nightmare scene uncovered Aug. 6 — other than the Evergreen Park couple accused of mishandling the remains of more than 100 people at South Chicago Chapel, 2939 E. 95th St.</p><p>“We’ve got to figure out a way to stay in front of bad actors,” said state Rep. Marcus Evans, the South Side Democrat whose district includes the parlor. “We don't want to make excuses. Whatever was done was not enough.”</p><p>It’s the second time in as many years lawmakers have been pressed to respond to ghoulish allegations against <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/07/owners-of-far-south-side-funeral-home-have-history-of-mishandling-human-remains" target="_blank" ><u>Clark and Johanna Morgan</u></a>, the operators of South Chicago Chapel.</p><p>The Morgans also ran a Chicago Heights crematory that was shut down by the state last year for mishandling the remains of about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/06/19/chicago-heights-crematory-bodies-death-license-closed" target="_blank" ><u>100 other people</u></a>. That prompted a new state law expanding the regulatory authority of the Illinois comptroller’s office, which, in a quirk of state responsibilities, oversees crematories in addition to its fiscal duties.</p><p>But Comptroller Susana Mendoza’s office doesn’t regulate funeral directors or embalmers, who are licensed by the Illinois Department of Financial and Professional Regulation under Gov. JB Pritzker’s administration. And apparently no state agency oversees funeral homes themselves, at their physical locations, officials said.</p><p>“We need to look at putting it all under one roof,” said state Rep. Diane Blair-Sherlock, D-Villa Park, who co-sponsored the 2025 crematory legislation and says facilities should be subject to quarterly inspections. “But neither of them are really set up with huge enforcement arms. … So I think that's where we need to look and say, where would this best fit, and who would be willing to take it on?”</p><p>IDFPR officials were “on site” in Chicago Heights last year, according to Mendoza's office, which had “urged IDFPR to take away Johanna Morgan’s funeral license” due to the crematory’s troubling conditions.</p><p>A spokesperson for Cook County State’s attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke said any potential criminal case never materialized.</p><p>“We met with [the Illinois State Police] and the comptroller’s office, which had referred the case to ISP, and recommended that ISP continue its investigation and consider the possibility of financial crimes,” the state’s attorney’s office said. “We have not been subsequently contacted by ISP to review a completed investigation for consideration of charges.”</p><p>In November 2023, after Laura Godina’s 91-year-old father passed away, she turned to Heights Crematory in Chicago Heights to have him cremated. A few months later, her mother, 89, passed away as well. She again turned to Heights Crematory for the cremation. But something always bothered her because her father was a much larger man than her mother.</p><p>“My concern is that the amount of my dad's remains in the urn is very small. There’s very little in there. But the urn for my mom is full,” Godina said in her native Spanish. “I'm worried about what they handed over to me.”</p><p>“I feel disappointed, because we hired them for a service. We paid for a service. I feel sad and guilty because I trusted them — I really trusted them — and they let me down,” Godina added. “I don't know how they treated my parents, who were the most sacred, most beautiful thing to me. They (Morgans) toyed with my feelings; they let me down. I feel so disappointed, so disappointed in them.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-750000" name="image-750000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8a8170c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6576x3691+0+348/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F9b%2F5f%2F4c7d85ee4c418ca432f5c0235d01%2Ffuneralhome-260811-07.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/65b55cb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6576x3691+0+348/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F9b%2F5f%2F4c7d85ee4c418ca432f5c0235d01%2Ffuneralhome-260811-07.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f4796d4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6576x3691+0+348/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F9b%2F5f%2F4c7d85ee4c418ca432f5c0235d01%2Ffuneralhome-260811-07.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Laura Godina speaks with a WBEZ reporter Monday about her experiences with Clark and Johanna Morgan at Heights Crematory in Chicago Heights. An attorney for the couple hasn’t commented.</p><p>Besides the 56 bodies found in South Chicago Chapel, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/10/cremated-remains-ashes-found-south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-95th-street-south-deering-decomposing-bodies" >authorities also found 56 boxes of cremated remains</a>, officials confirmed Monday.</p><p>A spokesperson for the Cook County Medical Examiner’s Office said they are storing the cremated remains found at the funeral home, and the Chicago Police Department is locating next of kin for these remains.</p><p>The medical examiner’s office had positively identified 11 of the 56 bodies found in the funeral home, and 10 of those families have been notified. Two bodies had been released to new funeral homes. Authorities were still working to identify the remaining 45.</p><p>“While IDFPR issues licenses and regulates funeral directors, and does not regulate funeral homes or crematoriums, the Department communicates regularly and promptly with the Illinois Office of the Comptroller, state and local law enforcement, and other local partners to address any form of known misconduct,” Treto said.</p><p>At an unrelated downstate campaign event Monday, Pritzker said, "the comptroller's office did what they should do with the crematory. It started probably seven or eight months ago,” Chico said.</p><p>“We alerted the Chicago Police Department. They’ve been there monitoring funerals. … They sent officers there to have discussions with the owners. We even asked the funeral home to provide security,” but it was never done.</p><p>Although he is horrified by last week’s discovery and the agony it has compounded for grieving families, Chico said he believes he did all he could at the local level.</p><p>“We asked them to be more respectful of the community they’re operating in. They said they were going to work on it. They were gonna be mindful. They were gonna be a good partner,” Chico said. “Bringing them to the community. Having the police involved. From my end, I did all I could.”</p><p>As of Monday evening, another mortuary was still advertising its business at 2939 E. 95th St. A person who answered the phone said the mortuary had a limited contractor relationship with South Chicago Chapel, but wouldn’t further describe their dealings. The funeral director of the mortuary was reprimanded and fined by IDFPR in 2019 "for failure to file a death certificate in a timely manner."</p><p>Property taxes haven’t been paid on the chapel the past two years, county records show. The manager of a company that previously received the property tax bill said they sold the building in 2023.</p><p><i>Contributing: Elijah James, Mariah Woelfel and Isabela Nieto</i><br></p>

entries.title: 2 killed in Armour Square shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man and woman were fatally shot Monday evening near a gas station in Armour Square, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 25, and woman, 22, were exiting a business in the 200 block of West Pershing Road just before 6:30 p.m. when three people in a silver Nissan car approached them, took out firearms and began shooting, police said in a statement.</p><p>The man suffered 12 gunshot wounds and was taken to University of Chicago Medical Center, where he was later pronounced dead, police said.</p><p>The woman suffered six gunshot wounds and was taken to University of Chicago Medical Center, where she was pronounced dead, police said.</p><p>The shooters got back in the car and were last seen driving eastbound, police said. No arrests were reported.</p>

entries.title: A dozen who will dazzle: A look at some top high school football stars on defense
entries.summary: <p>One of the hallmarks of old-school Catholic League football was its blue-collar, physical brand of defense.</p><p>The sport has opened up in recent years, but Catholic League teams still win championships on the defensive side of the ball.</p><p>So it’s no surprise this alphabetical list of 12 defensive players to watch in 2026 includes a trio from Class 8A champion Mount Carmel and a pair from 7A winner Brother Rice.</p><h3>David Folorunsho, St. Patrick</h3><h3></h3><p>A native of Nigeria who grew up playing soccer, Folorunsho is the No. 1 senior in the state and the No. 31 player nationally, according to the 247Sports rankings. The 6-3, 280-pound lineman is committed to Notre Dame.</p><h3>Tavares Harrington, Mount Carmel</h3><h3></h3><p>The 6-3, 185-pound defensive back is one of two Caravan seniors committed to Michigan, along with receiver Quentin Burrell. Heading into his third season as a starter, Harrington has career totals of 89 tackles, four interceptions and 16 passes broken up. He’s the consensus No. 8 player in Illinois and the No. 124 player nationally.</p><h3>David Hill, Homewood-Flossmoor</h3><h3></h3><p>An exceptional athlete who has played baseball and wrestled, Hill is committed to Wisconsin. The 6-3, 300-pound lineman is ranked 17th among Illinois seniors.</p><h3>Roman Igwebuike, Mount Carmel</h3><h3></h3><p>The 6-3, 225-pound linebacker is part of an impressive local recruiting class for Notre Dame. In two seasons as a starter, he has 199 tackles, 17½ tackles for loss and 6½ sacks. He’s the No. 9 senior in Illinois and in the top 160 nationally.</p><h3>Justin Johnson, Evanston</h3><h3></h3><p>Johnson is one of the fastest players in the state, as evidenced by the two sprint medals he won at the Class 3A state track finals in May. The 6-2, 180-pound cornerback is committed to Illinois and is the No. 11 senior in the state.</p><h3>Darrell Mattison, Morgan Park</h3><h3></h3><p>The Public League’s top-ranked recruit in the 2027 cycle at No. 15 in the state, Mattison originally committed to Michigan before flipping to Ole Miss. The 6-foot, 160-pound safety is also a game-breaker on special teams, returning multiple kicks for touchdowns last season.</p><h3>Kameron McGee, Brother Rice</h3><h3></h3><p>McGee, who has 40 Power Four scholarship offers, is one of the two consensus five-star prospects in the state in the 2028 cycle. A 6-4, 245-pound edge, he is ranked No. 2 in Illinois and No. 25 nationally. He had 48 tackles, 9½ sacks and 17 tackles for loss last season.</p><h3>Jameer Miles, Carmel</h3><h3></h3><p>The 6-3, 192-pound linebacker had 74 tackles last season. He’s the No. 5 junior in the state and the No. 52 player nationally. His 15 scholarship offers include Indiana, Ohio State, Oregon and Notre Dame.</p><h3>Brayden Parks, Brother Rice</h3><h3></h3><p>Parks is committed to Notre Dame, where his godfather, Chris Zorich, starred. The 6-3, 305-pound lineman is coming off a big junior season in which he had 60 tackles, 12 tackles for loss and 7½ sacks. He’s the No. 10 senior in the state and is a top-200 player nationally.</p><h3>Dareion Prescott, Bolingbrook</h3><p>The 6-4, 255-pound edge is a five-star prospect ranked No. 1 in Illinois and No. 17 nationally. He has almost 40 Power Four scholarship offers and was the first local star to commit in the 2028 cycle, picking Notre Dame.</p><h3>Jake Thies, Fenwick</h3><h3></h3><p>Thies had a game for the ages in December, leading the Friars past downstate power East St. Louis in the Class 6A final with 200 all-purpose yards, two touchdowns, 19 tackles and an interception. The 6-foot, 185-pounder is committed to Iowa as a safety.</p><h3>Caleb Tucker, Mount Carmel</h3><h3></h3><p>Tucker is known as ‘‘Bonecrusher.’’ A 6-5, 370-pound junior, he had 31 tackles, nine tackles for loss and 4½ sacks last season. He’s the No. 8 player in the state and a top-150 player nationally in the 2028 cycle.<br></p>

entries.title: DiJonai Carrington says ‘WHITE PRIVILEGE’ post goes beyond flagrant foul
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — Two days after the Sky’s DiJonai Carrington was ejected for a flagrant foul 2 on Fever guard Sophie Cunningham, she said her ‘‘WHITE PRIVILEGE’’ post was about more than what happened on that play.</p><p>Carrington wasn’t made available to reporters after the game Saturday against the Fever. But after shootaround Monday, she responded online to YouTube host Emmanuel Acho, who argued that the foul call was justified and could not be attributed to white privilege.</p><p>‘‘I’ve never once claimed that the assessment of the foul was white privilege (that was your assumption). Try exercising your critical thinking skills, I know you studied psych,’’ Carrington wrote.</p><p>‘‘I actually went to school, one of the top universities might I add, to educate myself on this exact subject. I would never use that term as a rhetorical weapon knowing the historical and social weight it holds without having the proper evidence to substantiate it.’’</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">I’ve never once claimed that the assessment of the foul was white privilege (that was your assumption). Try exercising your critical thinking skills, I know you studied psych. Furthermore, I’m the LAST thing from ignorant or asinine when it comes to speaking on “white privilege”,… <a href="https://t.co/mykXGTtiXJ">https://t.co/mykXGTtiXJ</a></p>— dιjonaι carrιngтon♛ (@DijonaiVictoria) <a href="https://x.com/DijonaiVictoria/status/2086912218457862229?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 10, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Before the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky’s</a> game against the Storm, Carrington kept her cards close to her chest when she was asked specifically what she meant by the post. But she made clear her concerns extend beyond the incident and said she already has raised them with the league.</p><p>‘‘I already spoke with people who potentially will have the agency to create the change that I’m hoping comes about from not just this incident, but ones in the past and that are obviously going to be coming up in the near future, probably,’’ Carrington said.</p><p></p><p>Carrington said she was not encouraged by her conversation with the league but intends to continue pushing for consistency. The WNBA did not respond to a request for comment about racism or unconscious bias in officiating.</p><p></p><p>Cunningham said after the game that she believed Carrington’s foul was intentional, done for attention and possibly meant to send a message after Cunningham flagrantly fouled Sky guard Jacy Sheldon last season.</p><p></p><p>Carrington rejected that.</p><p></p><p>‘‘It was unfortunate that I made contact with her in the way that I did, but it was never intentional,’’ she said. ‘‘And, look, it might happen again. That’s just how I play. I’m gonna always go all out. I’m not gonna just let an open layup happen. But like I said, I’m never intending to hurt anybody, regardless of the outside noise or whatever the situation may be.’’</p><p></p><p>Carrington also was asked whether Cunningham should have received a technical foul for her reaction after the play. Cunningham approached Carrington and gave her a small shove, which officials later deemed an ‘‘acceptable’’ reaction.</p><p></p><p>‘‘I would just love consistency across the board when it comes to things like that,’’ Carrington said. ‘‘Whether it’s the foul that I commit, whether it’s the reaction or retaliation, I would just love for it to be consistent across the board, regardless of the name on your jersey or your skin color or the score of the game, whatever.</p><p></p><p>‘‘I don’t think we’re there yet. That’s something that I’ve talked to the league about, as well. I think that will eliminate a lot of frustrations we all have.’’</p><p></p><p>Sky coach Tyler Marsh has been critical of the officiating throughout the season, particularly about what he views as a lack of consistency and accountability. Asked whether racism and unconscious bias need to be addressed in officiating, he said that was for the league to determine.</p><p></p><p>‘‘I think it would be ignorant to think that it doesn’t play a part in the grand scheme of society,’’ Marsh said. ‘‘But I don’t think it influences calls that happen with officiating.’’</p><p></p><p>He also backed Carrington’s assertion that the foul was not intentional and said the two have spoken since the game.</p><p></p><p>‘‘She knows where I and we are . . . for her individually and for our team,’’ Marsh said.</p><p></p><p>Marsh did not say whether he was disappointed that Carrington posted on social media after her ejection, instead acknowledging the power of social media and how quickly narratives can take hold. The WNBA and Sky did not respond to requests for comment about whether Carrington will face any discipline for the post.</p><p></p><p>‘‘I don’t think it calls for a matter of policing our players,’’ Marsh said. ‘‘But I think everyone is aware of what can arise from that. I think DiJonai knows how we feel.</p><p></p><p>‘‘She wanted to be out there for our team. At the end of the day, there’s a lot that has come out of it. There’s a lot of vitriol at DiJonai’s expense. There’s a lot that she has to deal with, as well. When we talk about protecting players, it should be every player.’’</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: 'Get your popcorn ready' because it is state title or bust for No. 8 Batavia
entries.summary: <p>Michael Vander Luitgaren, No. 8 Batavia’s third-year starting quarterback, knows how important Bulldogs football is to his hometown.</p><p>High school football is the heartbeat of Batavia. Vander Luitgaren’s young neighbors construct homemade signs every week and put them in the front window of their house. It is their small contribution to the town’s obsession.</p><p>“We say ‘one town, one team’ all the time, and that is how it really feels,” Vander Luitgaren said. “This community is so tight. The connection between the team and the fans couldn't be any better. Right now I have my head down and am focused on trying to get them a state championship.”</p><p>Vander Luitgaren has committed to Wyoming along with teammate Thomas Prescott, a tight end. But there is serious work to be done before heading to college. Batavia coach Dennis Piron, the affable maestro behind the Bulldogs’ success, says he is 99% sure this is his last season. Piron is a Batavia graduate and has been with the program for 38 years, the last 16 as head coach.</p><p>“If this is [Piron’s] last year, we have to make it a good one,” Vander Luitgaren said. “We haven’t really been talking about that, but however it goes, we have expectations. There are a lot of guys returning. It is go big or go home. We really want to win a state championship, and if we don’t, it is a bust of a season.”</p><p>Vander Luitgaren threw for 2,708 yards and 31 TDs as a junior. The Bulldogs finished 10-3 and lost in the Class 7A semifinals.</p><p>Prescott, Western Michigan recruit Darin Ashiru and NIU commit Brennon Zeng comprise the best receiving corps in school history. The offensive line is young, but running back Charlie Rosengren is an excellent receiver and a powerful runner.</p><p>“If we can keep [Vander Luitgaren] standing, we are really good,” Piron said. entries.title: 2 custodians fatally shot inside Mark Twain Elementary School, authorities say
entries.summary: <p>Two custodians were fatally shot inside Mark Twain Elementary School in Garfield Ridge on Monday afternoon in an apparent murder-suicide, according to preliminary police radio transmissions.</p><p>According to a statement from Chicago police, a 63-year-old man and 48-year-old woman were each found with a single gunshot wound to their heads inside the school in the 5100 block of South Lotus Avenue at 3:40 p.m. Both were taken to Christ Medical Center, where they were pronounced dead, police said. A weapon was recovered at the scene, police said.</p><p>According to police radio transmissions, a dispatcher said the shooting stemmed from a disagreement between two custodians. Both people were found inside Mark Twain Elementary School, according to the radio dispatches. One of them was found inside the school's lunchroom, the dispatcher said.</p><p>Both of the gunshot victims were custodians, according to Eric Bailey, spokesperson for SEIU Local 73, which represents custodians at Chicago Public Schools. </p><p>No students were at the school, as classes don't begin there until Aug. 24.</p><p>Trumaine Reeves, executive vice president of SEIU Local 73, said in an emailed statement that the "only facts we know right now are that two families have lost a loved one and our prayers are with their families, and the staff, students, and families at Mark Twain Elementary School."</p><p>Chicago Public Schools did not immediately answer a request for comment.</p><p>A neighbor who lives across from the school told the Sun-Times she saw first responders remove the bodies of a man, then a woman, from inside the school. The emergency response initially included four fire trucks and four ambulances, according to the woman, who asked not to share her name.</p><p>Several police officers and detectives could be seen in and outside the school Monday evening.</p><p>Additional information was not immediately released.</p>

entries.title: Chicago Park District to keep 20 pools open through Labor Day
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Park District is extending some of its end-of-summer aquatics programs through Labor Day weekend, keeping 20 community pools, 23 beaches and over 200 water play features open.</p><p>The expanded schedule means beaches and some pools will be open though Labor Day on Monday, Sept. 7. </p><p>The Park District said it chose to extend the closing dates of 20 pools in many neighborhoods with higher vulnerability to extreme heat, based on Chicago's updated Heat Vulnerability Index. entries.summary: <p>A 38-year-old man was was killed and another was wounded Monday night in a shooting in Grand Crossing on the South Side. </p><p>Officers responded to calls of a person shot around 9:35 p.m. in the 7300 block of South Indiana Avenue and found a 38-year-old man with multiple gunshot wounds, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where he was pronounced dead, police said. </p><p>Another 38-year-old man was grazed by gunfire in the right arm and taken to St. Bernard Hospital in fair condition, officials said. </p><p>No one was arrested and Area 1 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Sister Would Prefer To Skip Abusive Brother's Memorial
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My brother "Earl" and I always had a very bad relationship. When I was 6 and Earl was 13, he molested me. Actually, he took my virginity. My mother caught him but whipped both of us and told me I should have known better than to allow it to happen. Fast-forward to when I was 17. I woke up to find him lying in bed with me, stroking my face. I screamed for my mother, who said, "Oh, he probably came home drunk or something."</p><p>Earl was never nice to me; even on his deathbed he yelled at me for forgetting to take his house keys to my other brother as his daughter asked me to do. A few weeks later, I forgave him for everything he did to me, but the last time I saw him alive, I still felt his hatred toward me.</p><p>There is a memorial planned, and I'm not sure I want to attend. I'm the youngest of seven; some of my siblings know the history and have witnessed the animosity between us. Part of me wants to go because Earl was my brother, and part of me is afraid if I don't, my siblings will hold it against me. Another part of me feels a memorial is to pay your last respects to the deceased, and I have no respect for Earl. I don't know what to do. — <i>VICTIMIZED IN GEORGIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR VICTIMIZED:</b> From what you have written, Earl seems more like an emotional and sexual abuser than a brother. Your siblings have no right to give you a hard time if you skip the memorial. Remind them of how he treated you and how much you suffered for it if that fact has slipped their minds.</p><p>You should do whatever makes you comfortable, and if listening to your angry, abusive pervert of a brother eulogized would make you uncomfortable, stay away.</p><p>Because you didn't get counseling at the time he assaulted you, you might benefit from discussing your family history with a licensed therapist. To find one, contact an organization called RAINN (Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network). Its toll-free phone number is 1-800-656-4673, and its website is rainn.org.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My 6-year-old is enrolled in a Spanish immersion kindergarten class, and we are getting through it the best we can. We are an English-speaking household, so it is a challenge. The teacher is incredible. Her energy, dedication, spirit and connection with the kids is amazing. However, she is a cringe-worthy singer.</p><p>What she sings is nowhere near the melody. I'm not the only person who feels this way. Music is a big part of learning for the kids in this class, so this is a significant problem. As a singer, I can tell you that "tone deafness" is a myth. The ability to carry a tune can be learned.</p><p>I would love to offer this teacher singing lessons, for free, of course, but I have no idea how to approach it. A comment on vocal ability could feel similar to a comment on one's physical appearance. I brought it up to the principal early in the year. She told me she would look into it and get back to me, but never did.</p><p>Should I let it be, since these teachers, staff and administration have so much on their plates right now? We have been at this for nearly six months, and I really feel it should be addressed. — <i>IN-TUNE MOMMY</i></p><p><b>DEAR MOMMY:</b> Because the principal promised to get back to you and never did, it is possible that your kind offer fell through the cracks. Contact the principal again and ask how the teacher reacted to your proposition. If the response was negative, do not pursue it further. If she showed an interest, follow through.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p>

entries.title: As MLK noted, if a country stops counting its unemployed, it forgets them
entries.summary: <p>Three weeks before he was killed, Martin Luther King Jr. stood up in a high school gym in Michigan and argued with a number.</p><p>It was March of 1968. The government said unemployment in the Black community was 8.8%. King said it was almost twice that.</p><p>Not because anybody was cooking the books.</p><p>The country felt good about jobs that spring. The national unemployment rate was 3.6%, near the lowest since the Korean War. Washington D.C. called that full employment.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ec0000" name="module-ec0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>King was telling them the number was hiding people.</p><p>He explained how the count worked. It counted people out of work and still looking. It did not count the people who had stopped looking.</p><p>He described them plainly. People who had lost hope. People who had so many doors shut in their faces that they quit knocking.</p><p>“These people are considered the discouraged,” he said.</p><p>Add them back, he argued, and the true figure was closer to 16 or 17%.</p><p>That was 58 years ago. The count still works much the same way. Presidents have come and gone. The count has not changed.</p><p>Last week the government released the July jobs report. The country lost <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/08/07/nx-s1-5924786/employers-economy-labor-jobs-federal-reserve" target="_blank" >23,000 jobs</a>. It corrected May and June, erasing 103,000 jobs we thought we had. Over the past year we have averaged about 34,000 new jobs a month.</p><p>Almost nobody is being hired. Outside a few industries, almost nobody is being fired either. If you have a job, you are probably safe. If you need one, the door will not open.</p><p>﻿Then came the number that would have gotten King out of his chair.</p><p>The unemployment rate went down. It fell from 4.2% to 4.1%.</p><p>That happened because 264,000 people left the labor force. They did not find work. They stopped being counted.</p><p>You are counted as unemployed only if you have no job and you looked for one in the last four weeks. Stop looking, and you are not counted as unemployed. You are not counted at all.</p><p>Nearly six million Americans say they want a job and are not counted.</p><p>They are not lazy. They stopped looking because looking stopped working. They did not stop wanting a job. They stopped believing one was coming.</p><p>Thirty years ago I crisscrossed this country arguing against NAFTA. Corporate lobbyists said we sounded like Chicken Little. Two decades and 63,000 shuttered factories later, every exaggeration they accused us of had come true.</p><p>Those factories did not close on Black towns or white towns. They closed on both.</p><p>King saw it coming. He wrote in 1967 that there were twice as many white poor as Negro poor in America.</p><p>So he was not just giving a speech that night. He was building something.</p><p>He had marched to desegregate the lunch counter. That fight was won. The fight left was whether a man could afford what was on it.</p><p>In December of 1967 he announced the Poor People’s Campaign. The demand was jobs or income for all.</p><p>He meant to bring the poorest families in America to Washington and set them where the country could not look away. Not only Black families. White families out of the mountains. Mexican American families. Native families. Puerto Rican families. One caravan left Chicago on May 8, 1968.</p><p>King never saw it. He was killed in Memphis on April 4.</p><p>The campaign went on without him and mostly failed. They built a camp on the National Mall and called it Resurrection City. Rain turned it to mud. Police cleared it in June. No jobs bill passed. Nobody got a guaranteed income.</p><p>But King was right about the count. He is still right. A country that stops counting people finds it easy to forget them.</p><p>There will be plenty of arguing about these numbers. Arguing has never hired anybody. Only people hire people.</p><p>So here is what I ask of you.</p><p>If you run a business, interview the person your software screened out. Ask about the gap in the work history instead of assuming the worst.</p><p>If you know somebody who quit looking, walk with them back to the door. Say their name to somebody who is hiring.</p><p>If you belong to a church or a union or a lodge, find out this month who among you is out of work. Do not stop at praying for them. Make the call.</p><p>Dr. King argued with a number because he knew a number can hide a person.</p><p>Count them. Then hire them.</p><p><i>Ben Jealous is a professor of practice at the University of Pennsylvania and former president and CEO of the NAACP.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f50000" name="module-f50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Near the Obama Center, Han Cha savors the art of high tea
entries.summary: <p>“Do you want milk for your matcha?” asked Heiji Choy Black, the partner and operator at Han Cha, the Asian fusion high tearoom that she helped open inside <a class="Link" href="https://www.theastergates.com/project-items/stony-island-arts-bank" target="_blank" ><u>Stony Island Arts Bank</u></a> in South Shore earlier this year.</p><p>Choy Black recently debuted the tearoom, and companion bar Yunomi, with the artist Theaster Gates to enable folks to interact with Gates' ceramics and hopefully boost traffic to his South Side art center. Gates saved the distressed Arts Bank building from demolition in 2013 when he bought it from the city for $1, securing its status as a historic landmark. It’s one of several projects by Gates seeking to revitalize disinvested communities through his nonprofit Rebuild Foundation launched in 2009.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" Sitting in this beautifully restored room, consuming prix-fixe high tea from ceramic vessels worth thousands apiece, amid beeping timers coaxing rare brews to their apex, the query seemed to affirm that, here, hospitality matters more than dispensing tea dogma.</p><p>“For both Theaster and I, bringing people together and feeding them and giving them great drinks is something that really is so satisfying,” Choy Black told me later. “Our hospitality program grew out of our shared ideas about hospitality and how we move through the world, making it a deeply personal part of the project. There’s no hierarchy, in a way, to beauty, good food and drink, good ambience and hospitality; they all matter in equal amounts to both of us.”</p><p>That’s not to say that, inside Han Cha, you won’t be challenged to perhaps rethink food and drink pairings and exercise patience. It’s getting a lift from the much-abuzzed arrival of the Obama Presidential Center. But will the momentum continue? <b></b></p><p>My adventure began in the afternoon at Yunomi, named in ceramics-speak for the handleless tea cup pervading everyday life in Japan. A collection of stoneware cups and teapots crafted by Gates and his <a class="Link" href="https://www.theastergates.com/project-items/dorchester-industries" target="_blank" ><u>Dorchester Industries</u></a> adorn a wooden shelf on one wall of this dark wood-accented bar.</p><p>“I always return to the vessel,” Gates told “Ceramics Monthly” in 2021.</p><p>One of the singular features of this artist bar is an all-artist-created cocktail list that includes a Lavender Drop named after abstract visual artist Caroline Kent — with Earl Grey-infused vodka and lavender syrup — and a peppery ginger and lime-based gin Mule from performing artist Yaw Agyeman.</p><p>But I wanted to get a sense of Gates’ own tastes, so I ordered Theaster’s Gimlet. It came highly suggested: a docent who led me to the bar said he often drinks one when he stops by.</p><p>The drink, served in a tapered white chawan tea bowl with a lipped rim,<b> </b>was bracing and tart-sweet in the daiquiri style the gimlet has taken on since the cocktail revival of the early aughts. In place of gin, mezcal lent vegetal and smoky brawniness, with sweetness from blood orange syrup and a woody aroma from bourbon mist. It cost $18 (the cocktail menu ranges from $18-$20).</p><p>Choy Black said she set prices at both spots to reflect the “care, craftsmanship, and collaborative labor required to realize an experience Between 4 and 6 p.m., cocktails cost $10 and beer ($5) and wine ($10) are discounted.</p><p>“Drink in hand, they’re like, ‘Now tell me about the Arts Bank,’” Choy Black said.</p><p>Cradling my delicately ridged tea bowl, I gazed up at one of several restored arches featuring carved lion busts that accent the space. In the main gallery hall, mixed flooring materials collided beneath the soaring ceiling that contained hexagonal tinprint remnants from the old bank. An abstract mixed-media painting by Gates ran almost the length of the hall. Upstairs, the Arts Bank also houses a small gallery that’s currently showing a collaborative exhibit with Volume Gallery, and the sporadically open Johnson Publishing Library, which Gates acquired and agreed to safeguard.</p><p>Leaving the moody bar, I passed the DJ booth in the main hall and entered the bright and serene Han Cha. Off-white, round and oblong paper lanterns clustered above, while filtered daylight seeped in through gauzy white fabrics of different sizes adorning the large windows.</p><p>While conceiving Han Cha’s design, Choy Black thought of the importance of cafes as intentional gathering places in places like Seoul, where she spent time as a child, and how to encourage contemplative slowness through tea.</p><p><b></b> “When I go to a lot of cafes in the U.S., you see a lot of people working or being alone,” she said, “almost like the third space is a work space. Whereas in Seoul, there’s so much importance placed on cafe culture — connecting with people, enjoying food and drink and conversation." <b></b></p><p>Nine teas range from herbal tisanes to Korean black teas, Taiwanese oolong and Thai white tea.<b> </b>It took almost 25 minutes between ordering and receiving my first tea, partly because the restaurant was training a new brewer that afternoon. <b></b></p><p>My Red Chai steeped for five minutes at exactly 207 degrees before getting strained, poured into a glass carafe and carried to the table. Heady with Saigon cinnamon, it expressed gentler background notes of spicy ginger, cardamom and black pepper.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Han Cha serves a $75 three-course progression of locally produced baked delights over nearly two hours. The first course includes an English cheddar with Korean quick pickle, almond sujeonggwa drop biscuit and corn anju muffin with Gochujang hot honey butter.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Ellie Hogeman</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“It smells stronger than it tastes,” a woman at the next table said to her companions. I could see what she meant until I started sipping it with course one: a jewel box of crackers, cookies, pickles and cheese that our server playfully dubbed “an adult lunchable.” Han Cha’s vegetarian, mostly gluten-free menu was developed by former Momotaro pastry chef Jessica Vazquez and Marguerite Singson, who sells pastries independently under the Instagram handle <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/what_margie_made/" target="_blank" ><u>What Margie Made</u></a>.</p><p>A confoundingly moist, Sujeonggwa (Korean cinnamon punch)-inspired almond drop biscuit with warm spices tasted like a buttery brown sugar cookie when washed down with the chai. Its spice matched the heat of a tender cornbread ring studded with fresh corn and exhaling oniony chive notes. Umami-packed pickled cucumbers and aged English cheddar with meaty richness highlighted the tea’s inherent sweetness. Meanwhile, every bite begged for a smear of sticky-sweet, spicy, savory gochujang hot-honey butter. (Package that butter; I’ll pay an irresponsible amount for it.)</p><p>Vazquez and Singson make everything offsite, owing to the Arts Bank landmark status. Renovations to accommodate, for example, a stove and proper ventilation must adhere to strict preservation codes. This menu will be available until at least mid-August.<b> </b>(Upcoming culinary collaborations will include the artist and cake maker Hyun Jung Jun [<a class="Link" href="https://dreamcaketestkitchen.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Dream Cake Test Kitchen</u></a>] and Hsing Chen from the hospitality group behind Asador Bastian and Andros Taverna.) <b></b></p><p>The only time I felt the downside of Han Cha’s constraints was tucking into course two of the high tea: a triangular pair of photogenic tea sandwiches. Assembled on springy, porous Japanese milk bread, one packed rice vinegar-spiked Japanese egg salad, the other a magnetically heady Ottogi (Korean curry) pimento cheese. Time is of the essence with a bread containing almost as much moisture as tres leches cake. Its snow-white edges had already begun to shrivel.</p><p>By now, Han Cha was about half full.</p><p>“How close are we to the Obama Center?” the woman next to me asked after requesting the check. The server recited driving directions as if she’d given them several times before.</p><p>The woman turned to her companions. “Might as well make a day of it.”</p><p>Meanwhile, a pair of desserts arrived last to melt my earlier disappointment. A cloudlike banana s’mores in a sturdy, almost savory cocoa-sesame pastry case sat beside a mochi-esque honeydew canele with a bouncy, jammy interior beneath a boldly caramelized shell. Tropical, fragrant with burnt-sugar sweetness, it was a final bite worth savoring, like the last few drops of matcha — the best I’ve had in Chicago, I might add — and that cup.</p><p>I ran my fingers over the ridges beneath which the glaze felt thicker, examining the mossy-green tea against the white mottled with sunbaked orange. The vessel mattered more than I realized. This was as much an interactive art gallery as a fine-dining tearoom.</p><p>“Seeing the joy of people feeling the cups in their hand, to me, it’s truly so special,” Choy Black said. “So many restaurants have beautiful wares, right? This is just coming from a very different, deep artistic place.”</p>

entries.title: Insurance industry makes millions each day claims go unpaid, analysis shows
entries.summary: <p>A new analysis shows that delaying home insurance claims for just a day or a week can add millions of dollars in profit collectively for the insurance industry.</p><p>For each day of delays on home insurance claims, the industry takes in an extra $8.8 million in interest and investment income, according to an analysis by the independent financial institution rating firm Weiss Ratings for the nonprofit Consumer Federation of America, which looked at the money that home insurers take in as premiums as well as their investment income.</p><p>In Illinois, about 21.7% of home insurance claims in 2024 took 60 or more days to settle, according to data from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners cited by the consumer group.</p><p>Across all lines of property and casualty insurance — including home, auto, business and other coverage — the industry gains a combined $52.3 million in investment income for each additional day claims are delayed, the analysis found.</p><p>Douglas Heller, director of insurance at the Consumer Federation of America, said the money insurers earn on funds not yet paid creates a “perverse incentive” for them to drag their feet.</p><p>McHenry County resident Stacie Barger is just finishing a 17-month saga with an auto insurance claim.</p><p>Barger’s 2015 Buick Encore was totaled on March 1, 2025, when a driver pulled out of a side road off Illinois Route 134 and collided with her car.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a This is not a typical case and the duration is due to all these other factors,” Hincks said in an email.</p><p>First Chicago, which offers nonstandard insurance for drivers who don’t qualify for policies with more well-known insurers, had the highest complaint ratio of all auto insurers in Illinois, in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2024/10/18/nonstandard-car-insurance-consumer-complaints-american-alliance-first-chicago-insurance-united-equitable-american-heartland" >2024 Sun-Times analysis</a> of consumer complaints to the Illinois Department of Insurance.</p><p>At the time, Hincks said nonstandard insurance companies have more complaints because they insure high-risk drivers who have a history of accidents, traffic violations or poor credit and who have more interactions with their insurance companies.</p><div class="ActionBox Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="ActionBox-content"> <div class="ActionBox-title">Have you had a bad experience with an insurance company? </div> <div class="ActionBox-description">If so, tell your story to reporter Stephanie Zimmermann.</div> </div> <div class="ActionBox-cta"> <a class="Button" href="mailto:szimmermann@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email me</a> </div> </div><p>Heller said while money taken in for premiums and spent on claims and administration is roughly one-to-one over time, the insurance industry makes money by investing premiums in the interim. Warren Buffett, former CEO of Berkshire Hathaway, called this “the float.”</p><p>Heller said if insurers had to pay consumers interest on delayed claims, they might move faster.</p><p>He advocates a 30-day limit for insurers to pay the depreciated value of what was lost; after that, negotiations could continue on what else is owed.</p><p>“Don’t keep the check in your mail room an extra day or two,” he said.</p><p>The Illinois Insurance Association, American Property Casualty Insurance Association and National Association of Mutual Insurance Companies said in a joint statement the analysis “oversimplifies a complex claims handling process to score political points.
